items.body:
# Feature request

## Summary

The `Form` component supports a native submit button - `<button type="submit">` - but not a reset button:

```jsx
<Form onSubmit={() => console.log('submitted')}>
   <Field.Root>
     {/*  a normal Field.Control that renders an input */}
   </Field.Root>

   {/* works */}
   <button type="submit">
     Submit
   </button>

   {/* doesn't work */}
   <button type="reset">
     Reset
   </button>
</Form>
```

## Examples in other libraries

- [React Aria](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/Form.html#events) provides a reset button `<Form><Button type="reset" /></Form>`
- [React Hook Form](https://www.react-hook-form.com/faqs/#Howtoresettheform) supports a native reset button and also a `reset()` method via a hook

## Motivation

It's often useful to be able to discard all edits in a form and reset it to the initial values. This will could require Fields to additionally track the `initialValue`.

items.body:
Closes #5205

`autoHighlight` on Combobox and Autocomplete now also accepts `(itemValue, query) => boolean`, deciding on each query change whether the first matching item should be auto-highlighted. This enables hybrid token/free-text inputs where only certain matches (such as exact ones) should be selected when pressing Enter, while other queries keep the raw typed text. The signature mirrors the `filter` prop.

The decision is made in the pending-highlight layout effect rather than the synchronous keystroke path, since it depends on the first item filtered by the new query, which hasn't been derived at that point. The predicate reads the live input value rather than the derived `query`, which can still hold a stale `closeQuery` frozen for an exit animation when typing reopens the popup.

A function keeps the `'input-change'` semantics; it doesn't combine with `'always'`. The predicate only gates automatic highlighting, so arrow-key navigation can still highlight non-matching items. Costs +65/+50 B gzipped on the combobox/autocomplete entrypoints.

  - recommended patterns for async pagination

- Loaded more options on scroll

items.body:
# Feature request

## Summary

Add a Positioner for the Dialog component along with data attributes that expose the maximum available height and width (for example, relative to the viewport or positioning constraints), similar to how this is implemented in components like Combobox and Menu.
These attributes could be used to reflect the available layout space directly on the DOM node.

## Examples in other libraries

Within base-ui itself, similar behavior already exists in components such as Combobox and/or Menu
Both provide a Positioner abstraction and expose layout-related data attributes (e.g. available size), which can then be consumed for styling and animation purposes.
This proposal aims to bring Dialog in line with those existing patterns.

## Motivation

When a Dialog contains dynamic content (for example, content that loads asynchronously or changes based on user interaction), animating height and width transitions becomes difficult without knowing the maximum available space.
Exposing a Positioner and data attributes for maximum available height and width would make it significantly easier to implement smooth height/width animations

items.body:
Adds a virtualizer to Base UI: a component that renders only the items in and around the viewport, so a list over a large collection mounts a window of items instead of all of them. Built on #5414 — its commits are included here, so that PR does not need to be read or merged first. #5173 and #5414 are superseded by this one. ## The component ```jsx import { Virtualizer } from '@base-ui/react/virtualizer'; item.id} role="listbox"> {(item, index, itemProps) => (
{item.name}
)} ``` It is the scroll container, and it takes the collection either from its own `items` prop, as above, or from a surrounding list that publishes one. Inside `` it needs neither `items` nor keyboard wiring: ```jsx {(item) => {item.name}} ``` Those are the same component, and the two sources are what the three commits build in turn: virtualization for the combobox, then the same windowing as a component any list can publish a host for, then the standalone `items` mode. ## What it takes care of Items that are not mounted still belong to the list. Keyboard navigation moves through the whole collection, `isItemDisabled` on the list root decides disabled state for items that were never rendered, and every rendered item carries the collection metadata assistive technology needs — supplied through the list's own item component, or as the third argument of the item renderer for a list that has none. Heights are estimated until measured, and a static `estimatedItemHeight` is refined with the running average of the items measured so far, so the scrollbar settles without scrolling through the collection. Around that sits the geometry a list needs and an engine alone does not give you: scroll anchoring so a measurement landing above the viewport does not move what the reader is looking at, a retained row for a highlight outside the window so it can still be selected, scrollport padding treated the way a plain scrolling list treats it, and a geometry refresh deferred until a scroll gesture ends. ## Props worth calling out | | | | :--- | :--- | | `items` | The collection. Omit it inside a list that supplies one. | | `activeIndex` | The active item, kept mounted outside the window so it can hold focus or be referenced by `aria-activedescendant`. An index alone scrolls it into view; `{ index, scroll: false }` leaves the viewport alone for a highlight following the pointer; `align` says where a scrolled item lands. | | `totalItems` | Size of the whole collection when the items given are one page of it, reported as `aria-setsize`. `-1` for a size not yet known. | | `onEndReached` | Fires when the window reaches the end, for loading the next page. Once per arrival, arming again when the collection grows. `endReachedThreshold` moves it earlier. | | `trailing` | Content after the last item, inside the scroll container: it scrolls with the items and is measured into the scrollable height, rather than being pinned below the list. | | `actionsRef` | `scrollToIndex(index, { align })`, and `remeasure()` to discard heights taken under a layout that has since changed — a breakpoint, a font swap — while keeping the scroll position. | Keeping the scroll decision inside `activeIndex` rather than in a prop of its own is deliberate: whether an activation should scroll depends on what caused it, not on which item ended up active, and two separate props could disagree. ## Keyboard and accessibility The scroll container is deliberately not a tab stop. Focus stays in the input and the list is driven by `aria-activedescendant`, so making it focusable would put Tab into the list instead of dismissing the popup. To make that a complete keyboard path rather than a trap, Page Down and Page Up now move the highlight ten items at a time, and the list scrolls to follow — reaching items that were never rendered, which no amount of scrolling could do. That lives in list navigation, so **Select and Menu page the same way**. Automated checks flag any scrollable region that cannot be focused, so this container is reported by rules such as axe's `scrollable-region-focusable`. The docs say why it is expected and that it should be suppressed for this element: the rule cannot see the keyboard path that replaces it. The same reasoning decides what `trailing` is for. A list may only contain options, so that content must stay out of the accessibility tree, with the state it stands for conveyed by `aria-busy` and a live region. Interactive affordances — a create-new button, say — belong outside the list, where they are in the tab order and can actually be reached. ## Grouped collections A grouped collection — an array of groups, each with an `items` array, the same shape the list components take — is passed to `items` together with `renderGroupHeader`: ```jsx {/* ... */} group.value} renderGroupHeader={(group: ProduceGroup) => {group.value}} > {(item) => {item.name}} ``` A group header is a row: it is measured like an item and takes part in the same geometry, so the engine still windows one ordered sequence. Everything public keeps speaking item indexes — `activeIndex`, `scrollToIndex`, `getItemMetrics`, `getIndexAtOffset`, `isItemDisabled`, `aria-posinset` — and the translation to rows happens in one place. What makes a virtualized group still a group for assistive technology: each group's mounted rows are wrapped in a `role="group"` element named by its header through `aria-labelledby`, and when the header itself has scrolled out of the window it stays mounted, hidden, as the wrapper's first child, so the reference keeps resolving. Inside `` the header is a ``, which picks its id up from the virtualizer; `` is not used, since the virtualizer owns the wrapper. In a list of your own the header renderer receives the id as its third argument. Two things follow from the header being a row and the collection being filtered per keystroke. `estimatedGroupHeaderHeight` estimates headers separately, and headers never feed the running average that refines the item estimate. `getGroupKey` gives groups an identity that survives a preceding group being filtered out; it defaults to the group's index. The virtualization seam gained one optional field, `groups`, which a list publishes alongside its flat items; `` and `` do. Select can adopt it the same way on its own branch. Grid mode is still not supported. ## Table layout `layout="table"` renders the virtualizer as a `` inside a table of your own — the ``, the sticky ``, a `` and the scroll container around the table all stay yours — and the item renderer returns the `` elements themselves, with its third argument spread onto them so they can be measured. `activeIndex`, `scrollToIndex`, grouped collections and `trailing` work as in a list; group headers and trailing content become rows. ```jsx
…… row.id}> {(row, index, rowProps) => …}
``` The first version reserved the space of the rows outside the window with an empty row on either side of them, and showed a blank stretch whenever a scroll outran the rendered rows: the compositor moves the scrollport before the main thread commits the next window, and no buffer helps a scrollbar drag. The list layout never shows that because its rows sit in a sticky viewport moved by a transform, so the compositor keeps showing the rows it has. A `` cannot contain that scaffold, but it can be it: the section is now `position: sticky` and transformed itself, and a second `` after it reserves the space of the rest. Sticky header cells need a `z-index` above it. This relies on sticky positioning and transforms applying to row groups, which Chrome and Firefox support; Safari is still to be verified. Docs gained a Tables section with a demo, and there are `virtualizer/list` and `virtualizer/table` experiments. ## Testing Virtualizer 254 tests in Chromium and 183 in jsdom, covering windowing, measurement, scroll anchoring, the retained highlight, scrollport padding, paging, grouped collections (wrappers, retained headers, index translation, header estimates, React 17 ids), the table layout, and each of the props above. Combobox 1018 in Chromium, Autocomplete 81, Select 506 for the list-navigation change. Typecheck, lint, stylelint and prettier clean; error codes and generated API docs regenerated. Much of the behaviour here came from building a real application against the API and reporting what it could not express — the reason `totalItems`, `onEndReached`, `remeasure()`, `trailing` and the page keys exist at all, rather than being guessed at. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: [field] Validate once on Enter inside a Form

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

labels.name: component: field
labels.description: Changes related to the field component.

items.body:
When a `Field.Control` input sits inside a `Form` and is natively associated with it, pressing Enter ran the focused field's validator twice. The keydown handler committed validation, and the browser's implicit submission then ran `Form`'s submit handler, which validates every field again. An async or server-side validator on that field fired two requests per keypress, and `onValidityChange` fired twice.

The keydown commit is now deferred by a timeout and skipped when the form submitted in the meantime. `submitAttemptedRef` becomes `submitCountRef` (a counter) so each keypress can tell whether a submit happened after it. The deferral only applies when the input is natively associated with the surrounding Base UI form and the keydown was not `preventDefault()`-ed; standalone inputs and foreign-form associations still commit synchronously.

A plain "skip the commit inside a Form" gate is not enough. Implicit submission does not happen when the default submit button is disabled, or when a keydown listener prevents it, and Enter must still validate the field in those cases. The timeout fallback covers them.

## Notes

- Enter validation inside a `Form` is now asynchronous. Tests that assert synchronously after an Enter keydown need to await a tick.
- The `FieldValidity.test.tsx` assertion change (validator count 1 → 2 in `onSubmit` mode) is correct rather than a regression. A real submit bumps the submit count, and `onSubmit` mode re-validates on change after a submit attempt. The old count of 1 relied on the keydown loophole never registering the attempt.
- jsdom does not perform implicit submission, which is why the bug went unnoticed and why the new tests run in Chromium only.
- Bundle size: `@base-ui/react/input` grows by ~198 B gzipped, mostly the `Timeout` class entering a bundle that previously had none. Alongside any other Base UI import that already ships `Timeout` (field, select, tooltip, toast, …), the marginal cost is ~50 B.

items.body:
In a multiple Select inside a Field, `[data-dirty]` stayed set after the selection returned to its initial value.

## Root cause

The dirty check used `value !== validityData.initialValue`. In multiple mode `value` is a fresh array on every change, so the reference comparison was always true once the user interacted — even after deselecting and reselecting back to the initial items.

## Changes

- Compare array values element-by-element via `isItemEqualToValue` when computing dirty state in multiple mode, falling back to reference comparison for non-array values. This mirrors the equivalent combobox fix.
- Add regression tests for returning to the initial value, object values compared via `isItemEqualToValue`, and the order-sensitive case.

## Notes

- The comparison is order-sensitive, matching `CheckboxGroup` and `Slider`. Returning to the same items in a different order is still treated as dirty.

items.title: [field] Sync controlled value changes with field state

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

labels.name: component: field
labels.description: Changes related to the field component.

items.body:
`Field.Control` was the only Field control that ignored controlled value changes. Switch, Checkbox, Checkbox Group, Radio Group, Select, Slider, Combobox, Number Field, and OTP Field all sync through `useValueChanged` already. `Field.Control` instead drove every field concern from the DOM change event, so a value set from code had no path at all.

Two bugs followed.

**Dirty state never cleared for non-string values.** The dirty check compares the input's string value against a baseline captured from the `value` prop. With `value={5}` the baseline was the number `5`, so `"5" !== 5` held forever and `data-dirty` stayed set even after the user returned the field to its initial value. Array values failed the same way by reference. The control now registers the serialized value, so the baseline and the comparison agree.

**Programmatic changes left the field stale.** Setting the value from code, such as a clear button or a form library reset, updated the input text but not filled, dirty, or validity, so a resolved error stayed visible and a pending async validator for the old value could still publish.

The fix gives each mode one owner instead of running two sync paths at once. `useValueChanged` owns the controlled path, `onChange` owns the uncontrolled path, and `onChange` returns early when controlled. `Field.Control` now has the same shape as its siblings, with the residual difference being the mount-time DOM read that its uncontrolled mode requires.

Two smaller fixes ride along:

- `details.cancel()` in `onValueChange` now stops the internal handling. It was ignored.
- A controlled value the consumer rejects or rewrites no longer reaches the field state, matching Combobox, Number Field and OTP Field.

## Performance

Renders per keystroke for a controlled input, counted in jsdom (mount, then four keystrokes):

| Validation mode | Base | This PR | Number Field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onSubmit` | 1 per keystroke | 2 on the first, then 1 | 2 on the first, then 1 |
| `onChange` | 1 per keystroke | 2 per keystroke | 2 per keystroke |

Moving the work into a layout effect costs one extra render per keystroke in `onChange` mode. That is the cost every sibling control already pays, and `Field.Control` now matches Number Field exactly. The base column achieved one render by doing the work synchronously in the change handler, which is the second sync path this PR removes.

items.title: @base-ui/utils/useStableCallback calls Math.random() at module scope

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

labels.name: scope: all components
labels.description: Widespread work has an impact on almost all components.

items.body:
### Problem

`@base-ui/utils/useStableCallback` evaluates `Math.random()` at module scope:

```js
const useInsertionEffect = React[`useInsertionEffect${Math.random().toFixed(1)}`.slice(0, -3)];
```

In Cloudflare Workers, generating random values during module evaluation is disallowed. This crashes requests when Base UI is included in a server-evaluated bundle, for example React Router RSC client-reference or SSR chunks.

Cloudflare error:

```text
Error: Disallowed operation called within global scope. Asynchronous I/O (ex: fetch() or connect()), setting a timeout, and generating random values are not allowed within global scope.
```

### Why this matters

RSC frameworks can evaluate `"use client"` dependencies in server/client-reference chunks to build client references. The component still runs on the client, but top-level module code can run in the Worker runtime.

### Reproduction shape

- React 19.2
- React Router 7 RSC / Vite RSC
- Cloudflare Workers
- Import any Base UI component path that depends on `@base-ui/utils/useStableCallback`
- Request a route whose server/client-reference chunk imports that component

### Suggested fix

Avoid top-level randomness. For React 18/19, direct access works:

```js
const useInsertionEffect = React.useInsertionEffect;
```

If the computed-property workaround is still needed for older environments, it should avoid randomness during module evaluation.

Fixes a bug where the `onValueChange` callback was not invoked when the selected tab changed automatically due to external factors.

Previously, onValueChange only fired for user-initiated tab changes (clicks, keyboard navigation). It did not fire when:

- A selected tab became disabled
- A selected tab was removed from the DOM
- All tabs became disabled

Now, `onValueChange` fires in all these scenarios with appropriate reason values.

It also fires during initial render when no `value` or `defaultValue` is provided, and the component automatically selects the first enabled tab.

---

New reason values in onValueChange:

- `'initial'`: First automatic selection on mount (no value/defaultValue provided)
- `'disabled'`: Selected tab became disabled after initial render
- `'missing'`: Selected tab was removed from the DOM

The existing `'none'` reason is used for user-initiated changes.

items.title: [tabs] Consider 3D transforms when positioning the indicator

labels.name: component: tabs
labels.description: Changes related to the tabs component.

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

items.body:
Fixes `Tabs.Indicator` desynchronizing when the tab list is inside a 3D-transformed ancestor.

The previous implementation derived indicator coordinates from `getBoundingClientRect()` deltas and an inferred scale factor. That works for simple translations and axis-aligned scale transforms, but breaks with rotations, skew, perspective, or 3D transforms because bounding rects are projected viewport geometry and cannot always be mapped back to tab-list coordinates with a single scale.

### The component

The rect-based path is kept for transforms it can represent accurately, and the indicator falls back to layout offsets when the active tab or one of its ancestors has a distorting transform. Both offsets are computed and compared to decide which applies: the rect offset is only trusted when it agrees with the layout offset to within a couple of pixels of layout rounding, since agreement means no distortion is in effect. The layout offset walks the `offsetParent` chain for both the tab and the tab list and subtracts their layout positions, so the indicator stays aligned because it lives in the same transformed subtree as the tab.

Two things the comparison has to account for:

- **The active tab's own translation** moves its rect but not its layout slot, so it is subtracted before comparing. This is what lets the indicator follow tab-local animations such as `transform: translateX(12px)` or `translate: 50%` on the selected tab — the indicator is a sibling and does not inherit the tab's transform. Both the `transform` matrix and the `translate` longhand are read, with percentages resolved against the tab's border box.
- **Scroll containers between the tab and the list** move the tab on screen without moving its layout slot, so their scroll is subtracted from the layout offset. Otherwise the difference reads as transform distortion, the rect offset is rejected, and the indicator is left behind by the full scroll amount. The list's own scroll is excluded, because the indicator sits inside it and scrolls along with the tab.

### The pre-hydration script

The script deliberately does not mirror the component. It only ever uses the layout offset — no rect path, no scale inference — to keep the inlined bytes down, and it skips positioning entirely when the active tab carries its own `transform`, `translate`, `rotate`, or `scale`. In that case the component may position the indicator relative to the tab's translated position, so painting the layout slot first would show a jump at hydration; leaving the indicator hidden until React takes over avoids that.

### Other changes

`getElementTransform` moves out of `useSwipeDismiss` into its own module so the tabs bundle can use it without pulling in the swipe machinery. That is the only reason `ToastRoot` and `DrawerSwipeArea` appear in the diff — import updates, no behavior change.

Browser regression tests cover rotated, flipped, and 3D-transformed ancestors, tab-local translations including percentage `translate`, and a scrolled container between the list and the active tab.

Shadow DOM is not specifically supported, to keep bundle size in check: the `offsetParent` walk and the pre-hydration script both stay within a single tree. (The component's scroll walk does use the shared shadow-safe traversal helper.) Transformed tabs alone are very rare. Transformed tabs using shadow DOM even more so.

Fixes #4837

Demo: https://deploy-preview-4852--base-ui.netlify.app/experiments/tabs/tabs-3d-transform

items.title: [utils] Enforce store state key/value types

labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

labels.name: package: utils

items.body:
> [!Tip]
> Easier to review with [hidden whitespace changes](https://github.com/mui/base-ui/pull/5423/changes?w=1)

Fixes #5422

## Summary

- Tie store mutation keys directly to their corresponding state value types.
- Propagate the same guarantee through React store synchronization and setter helpers.
- Tighten popup interaction state syncing and replace broad `Partial<State>` accumulators with exact batched updates.
- Fix invalid call sites exposed by the stricter types and add compile-time regressions.

## Root cause

`Store.set` and several `ReactStore` helpers accepted `keyof State` independently from the generic value type. TypeScript could therefore infer the value without checking it against the selected key. `Store.update` and `useSyncedValues` accepted `Partial<State>`, which allows explicitly assigning `undefined` to required fields when `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is disabled.

Those signatures let the runtime store violate its declared state shape while selectors and component code continued to trust that shape.

Reproduction: https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-ghcgqkny

## Changes

- `Store.set` now accepts `State[Key]`, and `Store.update` accepts an inferred `Pick<State, Key>`.
- React store synchronization, controlled-prop, and setter helpers preserve the same key/value relationship.
- `usePopupInteractionProps` requires the common popup prop bags while validating component-specific state fields.
- Narrow floating-root synchronization to the popup-store capabilities it actually uses, preserving concrete state inference for specialized stores such as Tooltip.
- Popup, floating, and toast update paths now form exact updates while preserving batching and omitted-value behavior.
- Invalid call sites uncovered by the new types were corrected, including preventing Combobox event `type` metadata from being [merged into store state](https://github.com/mui/base-ui/pull/5423/changes#diff-30162b665077add067eff43f55765445b8292160513621f81fc186b6af941616R514-R525).
- Type-only tests cover wrong values, unknown keys, explicit `undefined`, state setters, popup interaction props, and popup open-change extra state.
- Direct tests cover the popup open-state branches that preserve active trigger data and control deferred unmounting.

## Impact

This is a breaking type change for `@base-ui/utils` consumers that pass a broad `Partial<State>` variable to `Store.update` or `ReactStore.useSyncedValues`. Existing valid object literals and exact known subsets continue to infer normally.

To migrate, represent broad partials as an exact known subset before writing them to the store. This prevents explicit `undefined` or unknown values from entering required state fields.

Store constructor initial-state parameters that still accept `Partial<State>` are deliberately out of scope for this PR and can be tightened separately.

## Validation

- `pnpm typescript`
- `pnpm eslint`
- `pnpm prettier`
- `pnpm test:jsdom ReactStore --no-watch`
- `pnpm test:jsdom popupStoreUtils --no-watch`
- `pnpm test:jsdom toast/store --no-watch`
- `pnpm test:jsdom ComboboxRootContext --no-watch`
- Focused jsdom suites for Combobox, Menu/Submenu, Tooltip, Preview Card, Popover, Dialog, Toast, and floating root synchronization

items.title: [popover][menu] Fix hover-out animations when switching between detached triggers

labels.name: component: menu
labels.description: Changes related to the menu component.

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

labels.name: component: popover
labels.description: Changes related to the popover component.

items.body:
When `openOnHover` is enabled, moving between detached triggers clears `instantType` so the positioner can animate to the new trigger, then sets it to `trigger-change` once that move finishes. That value could outlive the open cycle that set it. When it leaked into a close, the popup rendered `data-instant` and skipped its exit transition, so it disappeared instead of fading out. When it leaked into a later open, the entrance transition was skipped instead.

## Root cause

Nothing tied `trigger-change` to the open cycle that set it, and several paths let it reach a render it didn't belong to:

1. **The first closing frame.** `PopoverStore.setOpen` `flushSync`es a hover close *before* it resets `instantType`, so the closing render inherited `trigger-change`. Menu doesn't `flushSync` here, so its state update and reset batch into a single render.
2. **A late restoration.** The `runOnceAnimationsFinish` callback that restores `trigger-change` could fire after a close had already started.
3. **Closes that skip `setOpen`.** A controlled consumer committing `open={false}`, whether directly or after deferring a hover close, goes straight through the prop, so nothing reset the value.
4. **Reopening.** A popup that closed and reopened on the same trigger mid-exit kept its positioner mounted and its trigger unchanged, so nothing cancelled the pending restoration. A controlled reopen changes only `openProp`, so a value stored during the previous cycle came back.

## Fix

Instead of guarding each path separately, the fix enforces three invariants:

- **The `instantType` selector hides `trigger-change` while the popup is closed** (`PopoverStore` and `MenuStore`). It is derived at render time, so no closing render can show it, whichever path closed the popup.
- **Closing cancels any pending restoration and clears the stored value**, so the next open cycle starts clean.
- **A trigger switch is only scheduled while the popup is open.**

The trigger-switch effect was copy-pasted between `PopoverPositioner` and `MenuPositioner`. Both now use a shared `useTriggerSwitchTransition` hook.

There is no API change. Bundle size: +239B parsed, +38B gzip.

## Tests

The regression tests record `instant` on every closing render rather than asserting on the DOM, because a later render clears the stale value before `waitFor` can observe it. They run in Chromium only, since they need real CSS transitions.

| Component | Test | Fails on master |
|---|---|---|
| Popover | does not apply the trigger-change instant to a hover close after switching triggers | Yes |
| Popover | does not apply the trigger-change instant to a non-hover close after switching triggers | No (regression guard: a non-hover close isn't flushed, so the reset lands in the same render) |
| Popover | does not apply the trigger-change instant after switching back to the original trigger | Yes |
| Popover | does not restore the trigger-change instant after a reopen on the same trigger | Yes |
| Popover | does not apply the trigger-change instant to a prop-driven close after a switch | Yes |
| Popover | does not restore the trigger-change instant when a controlled close commits late | Yes |
| Popover | does not restore the trigger-change instant after a hover close has started | Yes |
| Menu | does not apply the trigger-change instant to a hover close after switching triggers | No (regression guard: Menu doesn't `flushSync` the close) |
| Menu | does not restore the trigger-change instant when a controlled close commits late | Yes |
| Menu | does not restore the trigger-change instant after a hover close has started | Yes |

Removing the stored-value clear on its own makes the prop-driven test fail on its reopen assertion.

The two "controlled close commits late" tests also assert that trigger 2 took over the popup and that `trigger-change` was restored before the late `open={false}` landed, so they can't pass without exercising the race.

Two guards have no test:

- **Scheduling a switch only while open.** It covers a trigger element being replaced mid-exit while a position animation is still running, and I couldn't drive that sequence reliably. It is kept because there is no move to animate while the popup is closed.
- **The open check inside the restoration callback.** Removing it leaves every test passing. A committed close normally aborts the callback first, but under a React 18 legacy root, `flushSync` can flush pending passive effects before running the callback. A controlled close committed there would let the restoration write `trigger-change` after the close had cleared it. That ordering is inferred from React's source and hasn't been reproduced, so the check is kept as a cheap safeguard.

## Scope

Earlier revisions of this PR also carried a hover-close grace window that let a popup reopen without waiting for `delay` right after a hover close. It has been split out: it's a separate behavior change with its own bundle cost and open design questions, and this fix doesn't need it. As a result, the handoff issue it targeted (moving from the popup to a different trigger sometimes doesn't open it) is not fixed here.

## Reproduction

1. Check "Open on hover".
2. Hover a trigger in the detached/multiple examples so a popover appears.
3. Hover an adjacent trigger. The popover repositions.
4. Hover out. The popover should fade out instead of disappearing instantly.

Originally reported on Edge on Mac, but it reproduces in Chromium as well.

items.title: [combobox] Add createItems collection API

labels.name: type: new feature
labels.description: Expand the scope of the product to solve a new problem.

labels.name: component: combobox
labels.description: Changes related to the combobox component.

items.body:
Closes #5228.
Closes #4735.
Closes #3865.

## Problem

Combobox treats each item as both the source data rendered by collection callbacks and the public value used by `value`, selection events, equality, and form submission. This works when applications want the selected record, but it is awkward when they render rich objects while storing primitive IDs. Deriving the ID on `<Combobox.Item>` is too late because the root needs values and labels before items mount, including for the initial input value, `<Combobox.Value>`, closed-trigger typeahead, autofill, and virtualization.

## Solution

API designed by @jjenzz.

Adds the pure `Combobox.createItems()` factory, which produces an opaque collection for the root's `items` prop.

```tsx
const users: User[] = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Alice' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Bob' },
];

const items = Combobox.createItems(users, {
  getValue: (user) => user.id,
  getLabel: (user) => user.name,
});

export function Example() {
  return (
    <Combobox.Root items={items} defaultValue={1}>
      <Combobox.List>
        {(user) => (
          <Combobox.Item key={user.id} value={user.id}>
            {user.name}
          </Combobox.Item>
        )}
      </Combobox.List>
    </Combobox.Root>
  );
}
```

Every API sits on one side of the source item / derived value split:

| Receives the source item | Receives the derived value |
| :-- | :-- |
| `<List>` and `<Collection>` function children | `value`, `defaultValue`, and `onValueChange` |
| `useFilteredItems()`, `filteredItems`, and the root `filter` | The `<Combobox.Item value>` prop |
| The `getValue` and `getLabel` accessors | `isItemEqualToValue`, `itemToStringValue`, and `itemToStringLabel` |
| | `onItemHighlighted` and `<Combobox.Value>` children |

- The collection lazily indexes its data, so labels resolve while the list is closed or virtualized without running accessors during collection creation.
- `getLabel` labels values the collection can resolve. The root's `itemToStringLabel` is the fallback for values it cannot resolve.
- Data may be flat or grouped, and accessors always receive leaf items. Filtering stays in the source item domain, while selection, equality, serialization, typeahead, and autofill use derived values.
- `filteredItems` remains in the source item domain. Its current window can resolve labels, but no previous window is retained.
- Derived values must be stable, unique, non-null primitives. `null` and `undefined` remain reserved for no selection.

### Why the collection is opaque

The collection intentionally has no public lookup API. Resolving a derived value consistently can depend on the root's current `filteredItems` and `isItemEqualToValue`, so a collection-level `get` could disagree with the root or encourage treating the collection as a cache. Applications still own the source data and can maintain their own lookup when needed. The opaque type also allows a public lookup API to be added compatibly later if a concrete use case emerges.

An [end-to-end test](https://github.com/atomiks/base-ui/blob/14987c4982258a28a7edd0064b02f115a2abaa61/packages/react/src/combobox/items/createItems.test.tsx#L191-L297) covers the #5228 use case.

## TypeScript compatibility

This PR narrows `filteredItems` and `filter` from `any` to the source item type. Existing code that passes object items while using primitive selection values may now produce TypeScript errors.

That combination was not consistently supported at runtime. Selection, label resolution, filtering, and equality could operate on different shapes. For example, the original #4735 pattern displayed the primitive value `"1"` instead of the item label `"Apple"` after selection.

Migrate these cases to `createItems()` with `getValue` and `getLabel`. Code whose items and selection values already use the same type is unaffected.

> [!NOTE]
> This is a type-level breaking change. Existing plain-array runtime behavior is unchanged, but code that relied on mismatched item and selection-value types may now fail to compile. That configuration was already inconsistently supported at runtime and should migrate to `createItems()`.

## When to keep object values

Use `createItems` when application state should store a primitive ID and looking up the corresponding record when needed is acceptable. Rendering and filtering still receive source objects, while selection callbacks, equality, and form submission use the derived primitive.

Keep object values when the selected value itself must carry metadata, for example, callbacks outside `Combobox.Root`, rich chips, or selected-value content requiring more than a label. With object values, `itemToStringLabel` resolves the label directly from the value, and `isItemEqualToValue` can match refreshed instances by ID.

Async loading alone does not decide which model to use. With `createItems`, `getLabel` can resolve an ID while its source item is present in the collection data or current `filteredItems`. For paginated search, keep the selected record alongside the current results, or provide an `itemToStringLabel` fallback backed by application data.

A possible follow-up API improvement would be passing the resolved label as a second argument to `<Combobox.Value>` children:

```tsx
<Combobox.Value>
  {(value, label) => /* custom rendering */}
</Combobox.Value>
```

This would make primitive values more convenient for custom rendering inside `Combobox.Root`. Because `<Combobox.Value>` consumes root context, it would not expose the label or source record to `onValueChange` or application code outside the root. Those consumers would still need an application-owned lookup or object values. This API is not part of this PR.

## Select

Select already accepts value-to-label metadata through its `items` prop and has no source item render/filter split, so this PR does not add `Select.createItems`.

## Bundle impact

The standalone factory tree-shakes when unused. The Combobox integration cost is tracked by the bundle-size CI check.

items.title: [select] Fix `alignItemWithTrigger` fallback with browser zoom

labels.name: component: select
labels.description: Changes related to the select component.

labels.name: type: bug
labels.description: It doesn't behave as expected.

items.body:
Fixes #4290


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6b3fb0d8-4c84-448a-8fec-458d87c2bf3a


CSS zoom looks to correctly replicate the rounding issues and I manually verified above in the recording

## Summary

`Select.Positioner` with `alignItemWithTrigger` could intermittently fall back to standard positioning at non-100% browser zoom.

The issue came from mixing zoom-scaled `getBoundingClientRect()` values with layout-pixel measurements used during the initial popup placement logic. For short popups, that mismatch could make the computed aligned height land just below the fallback threshold, so the popup would sometimes open below the trigger instead of staying aligned with it.

This showed up more easily in smaller selects like the docs styling selector, while larger demos were less likely to hit the same rounding edge case.

## Changes

- Normalize popup placement rects using Floating UI's scale calculation before comparing them with layout-pixel measurements.
- Allow a 1px tolerance in the fallback height comparison to avoid flipping due to subpixel rounding.
- Add a regression test covering zoom-scaled DOMRect values for a short popup.

## Verification

Verified on `localhost:3007/react/components/select` with synthetic page zoom (`document.documentElement.style.zoom = '0.9'`):

- Before this change, the docs styling selector fell back to standard positioning (`data-side="bottom"`).
- After this change, it consistently stays in aligned mode (`data-side="none"`).
- The larger select demo continues to behave correctly.

-   [not-\* variant](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v4#not-variant) — style an element only when it doesn't match another variant, custom selector, or media or feature query.
-   [Even more new utilities and variants](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v4#even-more-new-utilities-and-variants) — including support for `color-scheme`, `field-sizing`, complex shadows, `inert`, and more.
